figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: To match or not to match. Deep matchers are trained only on covisible pairs and thus return many confident matches between distinct but similar-looking structures, which breaks Structure-from-Motion (top right). FlexGlue tracks 2D query points across an image pair with subpixel accuracy and jointly predicts whether the two images are covisible, rejecting such doppelgangers with high confidence (bottom right). For 3D applications, FlexGlue is more robust than state-of-the-art matchers and disambiguates more accurately than the dedicated classifier DG++ (Xiangli et al., 2025) (left). We show that disambiguation even improves throughput by stopping early on non-covisible pairs.
figures.headline: Deep matchers trained only on covisible pairs return confident false matches that break reconstruction, while FlexGlue rejects such pairs with high confidence.
citing_sentences: 1), which matches sparse queries against dense context: given an arbitrary query point in one image, it predicts its subpixel correspondence in the other.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Architecture of FlexGlue. Each of the two images is encoded by a CNN backbone. The resulting dense tokens are fused by a Transformer that outputs context-augmented tokens. These tokens are decoded into overlap heatmaps and classify whether the image pair is unmatchable, in which case the inference stops. Otherwise, a query point in one image is turned into a sub-pixel coordinate in the other by interpolation of its feature, dense correlation, and match refinement.
figures.headline: The architecture fuses dense tokens of both images with a Transformer and exits early on pairs classified as unmatchable.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 2, a frozen pretrained CNN extracts features from each image, which we fuse across layers into a coarse grid of tokens.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Visual disambiguation examples. Left: Images overlaid with PCA of learned features. Center: Estimated correspondences pre-filtering. Right: We report the covisibility score after 3 and 9 layers in the top-left. Top: Our method correctly identifies a covisible pair. Bottom: We correctly identify challenging doppelgangers from various domains early and stop matching.
figures.headline: Covisibility scores at early layers already separate correct covisible pairs from doppelgangers, so matching can stop early.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Hard negatives of our LaMAR doppelganger benchmark. From left to right: different floors (CAB), indoor (HGE), outdoor (HGE), and cross-device (LIN) pairs. None of the pairs overlap, despite a high retrieval similarity (sim) from MegaLoc; $\Delta xy$ and $\Delta z$ denote the horizontal and vertical distance between the two cameras.
figures.headline: Hard negatives in the indoor benchmark show no overlap despite high retrieval similarity, across floors, indoor, outdoor and cross-device pairs.
citing_sentences: We therefore mine hard negatives, Fig. 4, with the off-the-shelf image retrieval model MegaLoc (Berton & Masone, 2025), selecting visually similar yet non-overlapping pairs.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Run-time on different keypoint budgets and layer ablations. RoMav2’s (Edstedt et al., 2026) run time is independent of the number of keypoints, but has a large overhead. LoMa (Nordström et al., 2026) is very efficient but scales quadratically, while our method is fairly efficient and scales linearly (left). Our method learns strong matching and disambiguation early on, while the run time grows linearly with the number of layers (right, black line).
figures.headline: Matching time grows linearly with keypoints for this method, while early layers already give strong matching and disambiguation.
citing_sentences: On the ongoing benchmark (Bellavia et al., 2025a), FlexGlue with 10k keypoints outperforms the top leaderboard entry by 8 points without extensive tuning, while LoMa exceeds the Kaggle time limit because of slower matching at this budget (see Fig. 5).
Fig. 5 compares the matching time as a function of the number of keypoints.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Detailed results on LaMAR-DG. AUROC and AP of FlexGlue and DG++ (Xiangli et al., 2025) per scene (a), difficulty (b), time (c), and device (d). Difficulty bins are tertiles of MegaLoc similarity per label, i.e., hard negatives are highly similar and hard positives dissimilar. FlexGlue remains robust on hard, cross-day, and cross-device pairs, where DG++ degrades strongly.
figures.headline: FlexGlue's performance holds on hard, cross-day and cross-device pairs, where DG++ degrades strongly.
citing_sentences: In Fig. 6, we compare FlexGlue with DG++ (Xiangli et al., 2025) on LaMAR-DG per building and group pairs by difficulty (MegaLoc similarity), time (same vs. cross day), and device.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Corrected ViSym test labels. Each pair shows the original ViSym label (Orig.) and our label (New). The original labels miss covisible pairs under strong viewpoint changes and mark some pairs of distinct but similar facades as covisible.
figures.headline: Corrected ViSym labels show the original labels miss covisible pairs under strong viewpoint changes and mark some distinct facades as covisible.

figures.caption: Comparison of matching modes. Left: Point-to-point correspondences estimated by our model, colored by epipolar error (green $<1$ px). Center: Keypoints colored by being matchable sparse-to-sparse (green), and keypoints only matchable sparse-to-dense (blue), highlighting the repeatability issue. Right: Sparse-to-dense correspondences. Especially under large scale changes and on low-texture areas, sparse-to-dense matching yields many more, accurate correspondences.
figures.headline: Sparse-to-dense matching yields many more accurate correspondences than sparse matching, especially under large scale changes and low texture.

figures.caption: PCA of the aggregated tokens. For each image pair, we show the two views and the first three principal components of their tokens at 9 layers as RGB. Our method learns structural priors such as horizontal and vertical lines, perspective, and planarity, and clearly highlights covisible areas.
figures.headline: Principal components of the tokens encode lines, perspective and planarity, and highlight covisible image areas.

figures.caption: Scene clustering on IMC2025. Image graphs recovered by our method with visual disambiguation only. Colors denote the predicted clusters and edges the retained image pairs. Top: landmarks are separated into clean clusters. Bottom: a single wrong pair (red) passes our filter.

Dense correspondences of FlexGlue, colored by their error from green (${<}1$ px) to red (${\geq}5$ px), with the PCK@1px per image, from the coarse readout, with our refinement, and with the RoMav2 (Edstedt et al., 2026) refiner. figures.caption: Dense matching across layers. Unfiltered dense correspondences of FlexGlue after 3, 6, and 9 layers, colored by their error from green (${<}1$ px) to red (${\geq}5$ px), with the PCK@1px per image. Despite being supervised only at sparse queries, FlexGlue yields fairly accurate dense correspondences. Deeper layers mostly refine matches and fix errors close to depth discontinuities.

figures.caption: Visual disambiguation examples. We show some visual disambiguation examples from the test sets of DG (Cai et al., 2023), ViSym-F (Xiangli et al., 2025), and LaMAR-DG (Sarlin et al., 2022). Top left is the GT label, right our covisibility score. Our method effectively distinguishes hard covisible pairs, but sometimes mislabels under extreme appearance or viewpoint changes, or when context is missing (middle row failure, wrong facade).

figures.caption: Qualitative matches. Correspondences of LoMa-G, SP+RoMav2, and SP+Ours on two pairs per dataset, colored by their reprojection error. abstract: To estimate correspondences across images, existing approaches match either sparse interest points, which is highly efficient but limited by repeatability, or dense pixel grids, which is robust but expensive. Furthermore, these approaches are trained with only matching pairs and thus often fail to reject unrelated pairs that exhibit visual symmetries, which is equally important in applications like Structure-from-Motion (SfM). We bridge these gaps by introducing FlexGlue, a neural network for asymmetric sparse-to-dense matching and disambiguation. Given two images and coordinates of points in the first image, FlexGlue estimates the coordinates of the corresponding points in the second image while simultaneously rejecting the pair if non-matching. By searching for a limited set of correspondences among dense pixels, our approach is both fast and effective at both matching and disambiguation: it combines the sub-pixel accuracy of dense matching with the speed of sparse matching, while rejecting incorrect pairs with high precision. Experiments on multiple datasets show that FlexGlue pushes the Pareto frontier in relative pose estimation and significantly outperforms existing approaches for SfM and visual localization. FlexGlue is publicly available at github.com/cvg/flexglue.

sections.body: The introduction argues that sparse interest-point matching is bounded by detector repeatability, dense pixel matching is costly, and learned matchers trained only on covisible pairs fail on visually symmetric scenes. It proposes FlexGlue, which takes query points in one image, aggregates context with a lightweight Transformer over dense tokens of both images, and predicts subpixel correspondences and pair covisibility. The contributions are an efficient sparse-to-dense design, joint matching and disambiguation at 4× higher throughput than dedicated disambiguation models, and an indoor doppelganger benchmark built from LaMAR.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Sparse matchers are fast but detector-bound, dense matchers are costly, and both miss visual symmetries.

sections.body: The related work groups prior methods into four areas. Sparse matchers detect keypoints independently and match descriptors or learned partial assignments, so their accuracy is bounded by detector repeatability. Dense and semi-dense matchers refine every pixel or coarse grid cells at high cost. Sparse-to-dense methods such as S2DNet and COTR either lack global context or refine slowly. Visual disambiguation uses retrieval shortlisting, sequential constraints in VidMap, or dedicated covisibility models that add overhead and generalize poorly. The section positions FlexGlue as aggregating context over full dense grids of both images and predicting covisibility within one model.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior matchers either inherit keypoint detector limits or add separate post-hoc disambiguation models; FlexGlue handles both in one network.

sections.body: FlexGlue takes two images and keypoints in the first image. A frozen ConvNeXt-B backbone with DINOv3 weights extracts features, which are resampled to stride 8 and processed by nine Transformer layers using self- and cross-attention. Each query is read out from the interpolated token grid by a shared linear projection, and its correspondence is a weighted average over the 3×3 neighborhood of the nearest cell, using 1.5-entmax weights. A matchability head predicts visibility in the other image, and a covisibility head at each layer can halt inference on non-overlapping pairs. A small MLP refines positions, shifting correspondences by 0.6 px on average. Before refinement, well above 80% of queries fall within 2 px. An indoor benchmark of 1000 pairs per LaMAR scene is also introduced.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: FlexGlue aggregates context over dense token grids and reads out subpixel correspondences only at query keypoints, with covisibility heads.

sections.body: Training uses eight datasets for 50 epochs of 150k samples, about 4 GPU-days on 4 H200 GPUs. Relative pose is evaluated on MegaDepth-1500, ScanNet-1500 and HardMatch. On MegaDepth-1500 the dense variant reaches 58.1, 73.4 and 84.4 AUC at 5°, 10° and 20°, against 62.8, 77.0 and 86.6 for RoMav2, with matching times of 28.4 ms and 73.1 ms. The sparse-to-dense variant with SuperPoint keypoints reaches 56.4 mAA@10px on HardMatch. On seven two-view benchmarks, the sparse-to-dense variant with 2048 DaD keypoints is reported as most accurate on all but IMC22. Disambiguation is tested on the new indoor LaMAR benchmark, where the paper reports a large margin over prior models.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Experiments show FlexGlue is competitive with dense matchers on relative pose at lower matching time, and it improves disambiguation, especially indoors.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes FlexGlue as an architecture that combines the efficiency of sparse matchers with the accuracy of dense matchers. It states that uniform attention over a grid with well-localized query points and visual disambiguation achieves the highest accuracy on two multi-view reconstruction benchmarks, ETH3D and IMC2025. It also reports improvements on all disambiguation benchmarks, on the indoor LaMAR dataset, on InLoc visual localization, and on the two-view HardMatch benchmark, while keeping competitive computational efficiency. The section gives no further numbers.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion claims top accuracy on two multi-view reconstruction benchmarks and on disambiguation and localization benchmarks, at competitive cost.

sections.body: The appendix reports inference cost: FlexGlue uses 1.2 GB VRAM for extraction and matching (0.7 GB for matching only), against 2.4 GB for LoMa-B and 3.8 GB for LoMa-G, and its readout scales linearly with queries. Keypoint detectors can be swapped at test time, and RaCo reaches 71.7 ETH3D SfM pose AUC at 1°, against 68.9 for SuperPoint. The ViSym test set is manually relabelled, with 3180 pairs reduced to 1184 kept pairs in a balanced subset. Limitations include errors correlated across queries, with most errors along the epipolar line (61.0 PCK@1px against 88.4% epipolar precision at 1px), and accuracy falling from above 90% PCK@5px to around 75% near depth discontinuities.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists inference cost, keypoint detector results, benchmark curation, training details, matching modes, and limitations such as correlated errors and depth-edge accuracy drops.
